original_question: Let T113(a,b) count tilings of the (a,b)-benzel when both stone orientations are allowed and all three bone orientations are allowed. Whenever a+b is congruent to 1 modulo 3, is it true that T113(a,b) = 1, so that the region has exactly one tiling?
target_in_paper: Section 8, Problem 14 (page 11): the type-113 question asking whether T_{113}(a,b)=1 whenever a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3).
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact type-113 tiling problem: both stone orientations are allowed, all three bone orientations are allowed, the relevant congruence class is a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3), and the claimed conclusion is T_{113}(a,b)=1, i.e. uniqueness of the type-113 tiling. This is the same problem posed in Section 8, Problem 14.
missing_details: The paper quantifies over admissible integers a and b for which the benzel is defined: 2 ≤ a ≤ 2b and 2 ≤ b ≤ 2a (equivalently, by symmetry one may restrict to 2 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ 2a).
The (a,b)-benzel itself is not defined in your draft; the paper defines it as a specific polyhex region, with an equivalent barycentric-coordinate description.
T_{113}(a,b) should be tied explicitly to the paper’s general notation T_{ijk}(a,b).
Type 113 means precisely: right stones allowed, left stones allowed, and all three bone types allowed.
The allowed prototiles should be named explicitly as the right stone, left stone, vertical bone, rising bone, and falling bone, with tilings by translates of these prototiles.
The question is meant for all admissible pairs (a,b) with a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3), not just for the numerical examples in Table 11.
No ambient ring/field, operator, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or 'for sufficiently large' clause is involved here; the hidden assumptions are purely combinatorial and geometric.
refined_question: For integers a,b with 2 ≤ a ≤ 2b and 2 ≤ b ≤ 2a, let B_{a,b} denote the (a,b)-benzel, i.e. the polyhex whose cells have centers (i,j,k) ∈ Z^3 satisfying i+j+k=1 and -(a-1) ≤ j-i, k-j, i-k ≤ b-1. Let T_{113}(a,b) be the number of tilings of B_{a,b} by translates of the five prototiles consisting of the right stone, left stone, vertical bone, rising bone, and falling bone. Is it true that T_{113}(a,b)=1 for every admissible pair (a,b) with a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3)?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, because in the case a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3) the Conway-Lagarias invariant equals the area of the benzel, so every stones-and-bones tiling is forced to consist entirely of right stones, does every admissible (a,b)-benzel with a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3) have a unique tiling by right stones alone?
justification: The draft is clearly targeting Section 8, Problem 14 rather than the neighboring questions: type 113 is exactly the case of both stones and three bones, and the condition a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3) with conjectured value 1 is the official formulation there. Section 1 supplies the missing definitions of the benzel and of T_{ijk}(a,b), and it also gives the Conway-Lagarias-invariant observation that explains why the congruence class a+b ≡ 1 (mod 3) is special. I therefore kept the question narrow and faithful to Problem 14, adding only the definitions and quantifiers needed to make it stand alone, and not broadening it to the unrelated 2-adic continuity problems in Problems 15-18.
